read.sections.0.heading.source: Everyday work can become a major subject
read.sections.0.heading.back: Everyday work can become a main subject

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art does not show only rulers, famous events or extraordinary people. Artists have also pictured farming, preparing food, caring for others, travel and rest. These subjects make ordinary labour, or work done by people, visible. The ways that artworks were commissioned, sold and displayed also connect their subjects with the people who could afford to own them.

You saw The Harvesters in Lesson 1. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565, and he arranged workers across a landscape. Some gather grain; others eat or rest under a tree. The Met's family guide connects the picture with the traditional theme of work through the seasons. Distant houses, a church and boats place the harvest within a larger world where people live. The labour of producing food and everyday life share the same scene.
read.sections.0.text.back:

read.sections.1.heading.source: A merchant's picture of farm work
read.sections.1.heading.back: A merchant's picture of farm work

read.sections.1.text.source:
The Met's collection record says that an Antwerp merchant commissioned the painting for his country house. He was its patron, the person who paid for it. The museum describes the workers as shown with sympathy, but idealised: presented as more orderly and perfect than real life. The painting's first owner and the farm workers in it had very different places in society. Its ordered plenty is one way of presenting rural life, not a complete record of it.

Bruegel's setting belongs to the southern Low Countries, including land that is now in Belgium. Antwerp was a major port and art market. The Met describes how trade and cultural contacts attracted artists and supported workshops. They also encouraged artists to make works for buyers beyond one town. A picture of the countryside could therefore belong to a business world in the city. This is context for the commission. It does not mean that every farmer shared the merchant's wealth, or that one painting represents all European life.
read.sections.1.text.back:

So the painting shows one view of farm life, not all of it.

So a picture of farm work could belong to a rich city world. This does not mean every farmer was rich. And one painting does not show all of Europe.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Almost three centuries later, Jean-François Millet made an etching called The Gleaners. An etching is a print made from a prepared metal plate. The National Gallery of Art's example dates to 1855. Three figures bend to gather crops left over after the harvest. This lesson uses the print, not Millet's better-known oil painting of a related subject from 1857. Fine lines, repeated poses and the way the figures sit in the field organise the viewer's attention.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum holds another example of the etching and explains its market. Millet began making prints in the mid-1850s, partly to earn money and to reach possible buyers. Pictures of the countryside appealed to middle-class ideas about the dignity of work. Such calm, reassuring pictures could exist alongside fears of social conflict after the upheavals of 1848. What an artwork shows and why its audience valued it are not always the same.

These examples connect art with food, labour, class and the market for pictures. A wealthy buyer could admire a picture of work without sharing the worker's life. An artist could make workers important while also needing buyers. Neither relationship automatically makes the art dishonest. It makes production and ownership part of its history. Dates, materials, patrons and markets help explain why pictures of ordinary labour belonged in collections as well as in the fields they showed.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Almost three centuries later, Jean-François Millet made an etching called The Gleaners. An etching is a print made from a prepared metal plate. The National Gallery of Art's example is dated 1855. Three people bend down to collect crops left behind after the harvest. This lesson uses the print, not Millet's better-known oil painting of a related subject from 1857. Fine lines, repeated body poses and the position of the people in the field organise the viewer's attention.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum holds another example of this etching and explains its market. Millet began making prints in the mid-1850s, partly to get money and to reach possible buyers. Pictures of the countryside appealed to the middle class, who had ideas about the dignity of work. Calm and reassuring pictures like these could exist alongside fears of social conflict after the upheavals of 1848. What an artwork shows and why its audience valued it are not always the same.

These examples connect art with food, labour, social class and the market for pictures. A rich buyer could admire a picture of work without sharing the worker's life. An artist could make workers important while still needing buyers. Neither of these relationships necessarily makes the art dishonest. These relationships make making and owning part of its history. Dates, materials, patrons and markets help explain why pictures of ordinary labour were in art collections as well as in the fields they showed.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Almost 300 years later, Millet made The Gleaners. It is an etching. An etching is a print made from a metal plate. This one is from 1855. Three people bend down. They pick up crops left after the harvest. This is the print, not his famous painting from 1857. Thin lines and the same bent shapes guide our eyes.

Another museum has a copy of this etching. It says Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints helped him find buyers. Many buyers were middle class. They liked the idea that farm work was good and honest. These calm pictures sold at a time of fear. People worried about conflict after the troubles of 1848. So why people liked a picture can differ from what it shows.

A rich buyer could like a picture of work without doing that work. An artist could show workers with respect and still need buyers. That does not make the art false. It means making and owning art are part of its story. Dates, materials, patrons and buyers all help explain these pictures of labour.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:

They pick up crops left behind after harvesting. This is the print, not his famous painting from 1857. Fine lines and the same body shapes guide our eyes.

Another museum has a copy of this etching. That museum says Millet made prints partly to get money. Prints helped him find buyers. Many buyers were middle-class people. write.example.source: Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints also helped him reach new buyers. Many of his buyers were middle-class people, not farm workers. They liked pictures of the countryside because of their own ideas about the dignity of work. So The Gleaners shows three people bending in a field. But it was made to be sold to people whose lives were very different from theirs.
